result.summary: Aristomenes is captured by Demeter's festival-keeping women at Ægila but escapes. At The Great Trench the Lacedæmonians bribe the Arcadian king Aristocrates, who leads his troops in flight and causes a Messenian defeat. Aristomenes then gathers survivors on mount Eira, where they hold out for eleven years.

scenes.title: Aristomenes captured at Ægila
scenes.summary: Messenians raid women celebrating Demeter's festival at Ægila. The women drive them off and capture Aristomenes, who escapes with the priestess Archidamea's help.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes risks captivity and death at the hands of the Lacedæmonians.

scenes.title: Bribery and its retribution
scenes.summary: The Lacedæmonians bribe Aristocrates. Pausanias notes later bribes at Ægos-potamoi and compares Sparta's later Persian-funded troubles to the Retribution of Neoptolemus.
scenes.stakes: Spartan honour in arms is lost, and later divine retribution follows.

scenes.title: Arcadian treachery at the Trench
scenes.summary: Aristocrates frightens the Arcadians, then leads them in flight, exposing the Messenians. The Lacedæmonians slaughter them and several leaders fall.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians face destruction and loss of their country through betrayal.

scenes.title: Siege of mount Eira
scenes.summary: Aristomenes moves the survivors to mount Eira, where they endure a long siege. Pausanias cites Rhianus on its length.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk starvation and conquest under siege.

Pausanias' usual name for the Spartans.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias claims Sparta first bought victory with bribes, a pointed moral judgement.

analysis.text: Pausanias stresses that dishonourable victory by bribery brings divine retribution, linking Spartan treachery to later downfall.
The passage ties the Second Messenian War to later events like Ægos-potamoi and the Corinthian War, and cites the poet Rhianus as a source.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias relies on the poet Rhianus of Crete for the war's length, and notes his unusual word for summers.

language_notes.text: The women, 'inspired by the goddess', fight in a divine frenzy; the Messenians are wounded by the women's sacrificial knives and roasting spits.
'Had the guilt of letting him escape' means she was blamed for it; 'old sweetheart' means a former lover.
'Lacedæmonians' is the usual name for the Spartans, after their region Lacedæmon (Laconia).
Ægos-potamoi (405 BC) was the battle that ended the Peloponnesian War with Athens' fleet destroyed; Pausanias says Athenian admirals were bribed.
The Retribution of Neoptolemus is a proverbial phrase for suffering the same wrong one has done to another.
'The Mede' means the Persian king; the Corinthian war (395-387 BC) was stirred up by Persian money against Sparta.
"Consternation" means alarm or dismay; "straits" here means a tight, dangerous position with no room to maneuver.
"Auspicious" means favourable; the omens from the sacrificed animals were read as unfavourable, giving a religious excuse for flight.
"Covenant-breakers" are those who violate a sworn agreement; the Messenians accuse the Arcadians of betraying their alliance.
The "double course" (diaulos) was an Olympic footrace of two stadium lengths, so Phanas was a recognized Olympic champion.
Rhianus' verse counts years by "summers and winters"; the poem speaks of twenty-two seasons, which Pausanias reads as eleven years.
Pausanias explains that the Greek word for "summers" can also mean ripe grass, so the poet's counting by seasons is why the total doubles.

context_notes.text: Demeter was the goddess of grain and harvest; women's festivals in her honour were common in Greece.
Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, killed old King Priam at Troy's altar of Zeus; he was later killed at Delphi.
Agesilaus was a Spartan king who campaigned in Asia Minor against Persia until recalled to Greece.
Andania was an inland Messenian town and an early royal seat; Mount Eira was a defensible highland refuge.
Rhianus was a Hellenistic poet who wrote an epic on the Messenian wars, which Pausanias uses as a source.

literary_notes.text: The great warrior Aristomenes is overcome by women using torches, a humble domestic weapon.
Myth is used as a pattern for history: a killer's own fate becomes a name for just retribution.
Pausanias moralizes, presenting divine justice as the explanation for Sparta's later troubles.
Aristocrates completes his treason by running straight through the very allies he betrays, making the betrayal brazen and visible.
The Messenians who expected to enslave the Lacedæmonians now barely hope to survive, a sharp reversal of their expectations.
The plain, compressed statement of eleven years of siege shows Pausanias' chronicle manner, moving quickly over long suffering.
